title: Alcohol, Antidepressant and Lithium Genetics: ADH1B, ALDH2, CYP2D6/CYP2C19 and DGKH
summary: Learn how the fast ADH1B*2 and inactive ALDH2*2 variants raise acetaldehyde, how CPIC uses CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 results to change the dose or the drug for tricyclics and SSRIs, and what DGKH does and does not tell you about lithium.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 73 Hits 5, 6 and 9, checked against Edenberg 2007, the CPIC tricyclic (Hicks 2017) and SSRI (Bousman 2023) guidelines (full text), Baum 2008 (abstract only; the full-text page was blocked by a captcha/403 in the fact-check), Alda 2015 and Vecera 2021. Hit 5 gives the ADH1B change as “His→Arg at 48”; Edenberg gives the fast ADH1B*2 allele as His48 in place of the reference Arg48, so the lesson teaches Arg48→His48 (register rv-ch73-adh1b-direction). Hit 6 says poor and ultrarapid metabolizers “need dose adjustments”; CPIC often recommends a different drug instead (rv-ch73-antidepressant-alt-drug). Hit 9: DGKH came from a case-control bipolar risk GWAS, not a lithium-response study, and the claim that lithium is the only mood stabilizer thoroughly examined pharmacogenomically was not verified and is not taught (rv-ch73-dgkh-lithium). Not taught: alcohol use disorder prevalence/heritability, KCNC1/KCNG2, calmodulin, CNVs.

objectives: Explain how ADH1B*2 and ALDH2*2 change acetaldehyde levels and why both protect against alcohol dependence.
Apply CPIC recommendations for CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 phenotypes to tricyclics, citalopram/escitalopram and paroxetine, including when a different drug is advised.
State what DGKH encodes, how it was identified, and why it is not a validated lithium-response test.

scenes.title: Three genotypes, three questions
scenes.altText: Invented scenario with three patient cards: (1) a young adult who flushes, feels nauseated and has a racing heart after one drink; (2) a patient with depression, genotyped as a CYP2C19 ultrarapid metabolizer, about to start escitalopram; (3) a patient with bipolar disorder starting lithium who asks whether “the lithium gene” DGKH predicts response. Question token: “Which gene, which direction, what action?”

cues.text: Invented cases. One: a young adult flushes, feels sick and has a racing heart after a single drink.
Two: a patient with depression is a CYP2C19 ultrarapid metabolizer and is about to start escitalopram. Three: a patient starting lithium asks about a gene called DGKH.
For each one: which gene, which direction, and what should happen next?

props.label: Which gene, which direction, what action?

scenes.title: Two enzymes, one toxic middle step
scenes.altText: Schematic pathway: ethanol → (alcohol dehydrogenase, ADH) → acetaldehyde → (aldehyde dehydrogenase, mainly mitochondrial ALDH2) → acetate. Variant cards: ADH1B*2 carries histidine at position 48 (reference ADH1B*1 has arginine; older literature numbers it 47); β2 subunit turnover is 70- to 80-fold higher than β1, so ethanol is turned into acetaldehyde faster. ALDH2*2: lysine replaces glutamate at position 504 (487 in the mature enzyme); the enzyme is essentially inactive and nearly dominant, so heterozygotes have almost no liver ALDH2 activity. Acetaldehyde accumulates → flushing, nausea, tachycardia, like the disulfiram reaction. Both variants protect against alcohol dependence.

cues.text: Ethanol is cleared in two steps. Alcohol dehydrogenase turns it into acetaldehyde, a toxic middle product, and mitochondrial ALDH2 turns acetaldehyde into acetate.
The fast ADH1B variant, ADH1B star 2, has histidine instead of arginine at position 48. Its enzyme turns over seventy to eighty times faster, so acetaldehyde is made faster.
The ALDH2 star 2 variant swaps glutamate for lysine at position 504, called 487 in the mature enzyme. It is nearly inactive, and nearly dominant: one copy leaves almost no liver ALDH2 activity.
Acetaldehyde builds up, causing flushing, nausea and a fast heart rate, much like disulfiram. Both variants protect against alcohol dependence.

props.label: Flushing · nausea · tachycardia → protective vs dependence

scenes.title: Antidepressants: dose change or different drug
scenes.altText: CPIC cards. Tricyclics (2016 update): tertiary amines such as amitriptyline are demethylated mainly by CYP2C19 to secondary amines (nortriptyline, desipramine); both are hydroxylated by CYP2D6 to less active metabolites. CYP2D6 ultrarapid → avoid tricyclic (likely lack of efficacy); poor → avoid (side effects); intermediate → consider 25% lower starting dose. CYP2C19 ultrarapid/rapid → avoid tertiary amine; poor → avoid tertiary amine and consider a drug not metabolized by CYP2C19, or, if a tertiary amine is used, consider a 50% lower starting dose plus therapeutic drug monitoring. SSRIs (2023): citalopram/escitalopram CYP2C19 ultrarapid → consider an alternative not predominantly metabolized by CYP2C19; poor → alternative preferred, or lower start and 50% lower maintenance dose. Paroxetine CYP2D6 ultrarapid → alternative drug; poor → 50% lower starting dose. No recommendations from SLC6A4 or HTR2A genotype.

cues.text: For tricyclics, CYP2C19 demethylates tertiary amines like amitriptyline into secondary amines like nortriptyline. CYP2D6 then hydroxylates both into less active products.

CPIC advises avoiding tricyclics in CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizers, who may not respond, and in poor metabolizers, who risk side effects. CYP2D6 intermediate metabolizers can start at a quarter less, with drug monitoring.

For SSRIs, a CYP2C19 ultrarapid metabolizer starting citalopram or escitalopram should be considered for a different antidepressant not mainly cleared by CYP2C19. Poor metabolizers: an alternative is preferred, or a lower dose.
Paroxetine depends on CYP2D6: ultrarapid, choose another drug; poor, halve the starting dose. So the action is sometimes a dose change and sometimes a different drug.

props.label: Action = dose change OR a different drug

scenes.title: Lithium, DGKH and the hook answers
scenes.altText: Lithium card: first-line treatment for preventing manic and depressive episodes of bipolar disorder; it inhibits inositol monophosphatase (IMPase) and inositol polyphosphate-1-phosphatase, lowering inositol and IP3; response varies (about 30% excellent responders; up to 40% fail to respond or cannot tolerate it). DGKH card: encodes diacylglycerol kinase eta, a protein in the lithium-sensitive phosphatidylinositol pathway; it was implicated by the first genome-wide association study of bipolar disorder (Baum 2008), a case-control study of disease risk rather than of lithium response. No lithium-response genetic finding had been replicated in two samples of 200 or more patients as of Alda 2015. Hook answers: (1) ALDH2*2, loss of function, acetaldehyde accumulates; (2) escitalopram in a CYP2C19 ultrarapid metabolizer: consider an alternative antidepressant; (3) DGKH is a bipolar risk signal in a lithium-sensitive pathway, not a validated lithium-response test.

cues.text: Lithium is still first-line for preventing manic and depressive episodes. It inhibits inositol monophosphatase, lowering inositol, and response varies: about three in ten patients respond excellently.

DGKH encodes diacylglycerol kinase eta, a protein in the lithium-sensitive phosphatidylinositol pathway. It came from a case-control genome-wide study of bipolar disorder risk, not a study of lithium response.
Hook answers. One: ALDH2 star 2, a loss of function that lets acetaldehyde accumulate. Two: consider an antidepressant not mainly cleared by CYP2C19.
Three: DGKH is a bipolar risk signal in a lithium-sensitive pathway, not a validated test of lithium response.

props.title: Hook answers
lines: 3 DGKH: risk signal, not a lithium-response test

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “ADH1B His→Arg at 48 is the fast allele” (✓ the fast ADH1B*2 allele has His48 in place of the reference Arg48); “Poor or ultrarapid metabolizer = just adjust the dose” (✓ CPIC often recommends a different drug, such as escitalopram in CYP2C19 ultrarapid or tricyclics in CYP2D6 poor and ultrarapid metabolizers); “DGKH was found as a lithium-response gene” (✓ it came from a case-control GWAS of bipolar disorder risk).

cues.text: Trap one: ADH1B histidine-to-arginine is the fast allele. No: the fast allele, star 2, carries histidine where the reference has arginine.
Trap two: a poor or ultrarapid metabolizer just needs a dose change. No: CPIC often recommends a different drug.
Trap three: DGKH was found by studying lithium response. No: it came from a study of bipolar disorder risk.

props.title: ✗ “PM or UM: just change the dose.”

scenes.title: Fast tap, blocked drain
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “ADH1B*2 is a FAST TAP filling the sink with acetaldehyde; ALDH2*2 is a BLOCKED DRAIN. Either way the sink overflows and the face flushes.” Tokens: fast tap = ADH1B*2 (His48) · blocked drain = ALDH2*2 (Lys504) · overflow = flushing. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: ADH1B star 2 is a fast tap filling the sink with acetaldehyde. ALDH2 star 2 is a blocked drain. Either way, the sink overflows and the face flushes.
Where it breaks: the blocked drain is nearly dominant, so one copy is enough; the fast tap protects less in Europeans than in Asians; and the sink says nothing about antidepressants or lithium.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: ALDH2*2 nearly dominant: one copy enough
Says nothing about CYP or lithium genes

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “ADH1B*2 (His48) fast · ALDH2*2 (Lys504) nearly inactive → acetaldehyde, flushing”, “CYP2D6/CYP2C19 → dose change or different drug · DGKH = bipolar risk, lithium pathway”.

cues.text: Fast ADH1B and nearly inactive ALDH2 both raise acetaldehyde and cause flushing, CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 results can call for a different antidepressant rather than only a new dose, and DGKH is a bipolar risk gene in the lithium-sensitive pathway rather than a response test.

props.label: ADH1B*2 His48 fast · ALDH2*2 Lys504 nearly inactive → acetaldehyde
CYP2D6/2C19 → dose OR drug · DGKH = risk, Li pathway

explanation.what: Plain language: alcohol is broken down in two steps, and the middle product, acetaldehyde, causes flushing; one common variant speeds up the first step and another nearly stops the second. Antidepressant levels depend on two liver enzymes, so a gene test can mean a different dose or a different drug. Lithium works through a signalling pathway, and one gene in that pathway turned up in a bipolar risk study. Scientific terms: alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH1B*2, Arg48His), aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2*2, Glu504Lys; 487 in the mature enzyme), acetaldehyde, CYP2D6, CYP2C19, metabolizer phenotype, tertiary and secondary amine tricyclics, CPIC, inositol monophosphatase, diacylglycerol kinase eta (DGKH), genome-wide association study.
explanation.why: Fast ADH1B makes acetaldehyde faster and inactive ALDH2 clears it slowly; the aversive reaction protects against alcohol dependence. CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 activity sets antidepressant exposure, so extreme phenotypes risk failure or side effects. DGKH sits in the phosphatidylinositol pathway that lithium affects, which is why it is discussed with lithium.
explanation.measure: ADH1B*2: β2 turnover 70–80-fold higher than β1. ALDH2*2 heterozygotes: almost no liver ALDH2 activity. CPIC tricyclics: CYP2D6 ultrarapid or poor → avoid; intermediate → 25% lower start; CYP2C19 ultrarapid/rapid → avoid tertiary amines; poor → avoid tertiary amines, or if one is used, 50% lower start with drug monitoring. CPIC SSRIs: citalopram/escitalopram CYP2C19 ultrarapid → alternative; poor → alternative preferred or 50% lower maintenance dose; paroxetine CYP2D6 ultrarapid → alternative, poor → 50% lower start. No SLC6A4/HTR2A recommendations. Lithium: about 30% excellent responders.
explanation.differs: ADH1B*2 (gain, faster acetaldehyde production) vs ALDH2*2 (loss, slower acetaldehyde removal); dose change vs alternative drug; GWAS of disease risk vs study of drug response.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: name the variant behind alcohol flushing, choose the CPIC action for a metabolizer phenotype, or identify DGKH as diacylglycerol kinase eta in the lithium-sensitive pathway.

mnemonic.text: ADH1B*2 is a FAST TAP filling the sink with acetaldehyde; ALDH2*2 is a BLOCKED DRAIN. Either way the sink overflows and the face flushes.
mnemonic.explanation: Links both alcohol variants to the same toxic intermediate.
mnemonic.limitation: ALDH2*2 is nearly dominant, so one copy is enough to block the drain, which the sink image does not show; ADH1B*2 protection is weaker in Europeans than in Asians; the image says nothing about antidepressant or lithium genetics.

analogyLimitations: CPIC recommendations summarised for selected drugs only; other guidelines may differ.
takeaway: Fast ADH1B and nearly inactive ALDH2 both raise acetaldehyde and cause flushing, CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 results can call for a different antidepressant rather than only a new dose, and DGKH is a bipolar risk gene in the lithium-sensitive pathway rather than a response test.

questions.stem: A young adult has intense facial flushing, nausea and tachycardia after one alcoholic drink. Which variant best explains this?

options.text: ALDH2*2 (Glu504Lys; Glu487Lys in the mature enzyme), loss of function
options.rationale: Correct. The nearly inactive, nearly dominant ALDH2*2 enzyme lets acetaldehyde accumulate, causing the flush reaction.
Incorrect. Arg48 is the reference, slower ADH1B form; the flush reaction after small amounts of alcohol is described in ALDH2*2 carriers.
Incorrect. CYP2D6 metabolizes drugs such as tricyclics; acetaldehyde is cleared mainly by mitochondrial ALDH2.
Incorrect. DGKH was implicated in bipolar disorder risk, not alcohol metabolism.

questions.stem: A patient with depression is a CYP2C19 ultrarapid metabolizer and escitalopram is planned. What does the 2023 CPIC guideline recommend?

options.text: Consider a clinically appropriate antidepressant not predominantly metabolized by CYP2C19
options.rationale: Correct. CPIC gives a strong recommendation to consider an alternative in CYP2C19 ultrarapid metabolizers.

options.text: Start at 50% of the usual dose
options.rationale: Incorrect. A lower dose is the fallback for poor metabolizers who still take the drug; ultrarapid metabolizers clear it faster, so a cut would make levels even lower.

options.text: Choose the drug by SLC6A4 genotype
options.rationale: Incorrect. CPIC makes no recommendations based on SLC6A4 or HTR2A genotype.

options.text: Use the standard dose; CYP2C19 does not affect escitalopram
options.rationale: Incorrect. Citalopram and escitalopram are CYP2C19 substrates covered by the guideline.

questions.stem: Which statement about DGKH is supported by the study that first implicated it?

options.text: It encodes diacylglycerol kinase eta, in the lithium-sensitive phosphatidylinositol pathway, and was found in a GWAS of bipolar disorder risk
options.rationale: Correct. Baum 2008 was a case-control study of bipolar disorder risk, and it describes DGKH as a key protein in the lithium-sensitive pathway.

options.text: It encodes inositol monophosphatase, the enzyme lithium inhibits
options.rationale: Incorrect. Lithium inhibits inositol monophosphatase, but DGKH encodes diacylglycerol kinase eta.

options.text: It is a validated test that predicts lithium response
options.rationale: Incorrect. The original study looked at disease risk, not lithium response, and no lithium-response genetic finding had been robustly replicated as of 2015.

options.text: It is a single gene of large effect that causes bipolar disorder
options.rationale: Incorrect. The study found modest effects and suggested bipolar disorder may be polygenic.

ADH1B*2 = His48 in place of reference Arg48; 70–80-fold higher turnover; protective, weaker in Europeans.

claims.text: ALDH2*2 = Glu504Lys (487 mature), nearly inactive and nearly dominant; strongly protective.
CPIC tricyclic recommendations by CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 phenotype; tertiary vs secondary amine metabolism.
CPIC SSRI recommendations for citalopram/escitalopram (CYP2C19) and paroxetine (CYP2D6); no SLC6A4/HTR2A recommendations.
Lithium first-line for bipolar maintenance; inhibits IMPase; about 30% excellent responders.

DGKH encodes diacylglycerol kinase eta in the lithium-sensitive phosphatidylinositol pathway; identified in a case-control GWAS of bipolar disorder risk, not a lithium-response study; not a validated lithium-response test.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 73 Hit 5 (and its 5-Second Recall) gives the ADH1B change as “His→Arg at 48 = gain of function”. Edenberg 2007 gives the reference ADH1B*1 as Arg48 and the fast ADH1B*2 allele as His48, so the gain-of-function change is Arg48→His48. The lesson teaches Arg48→His48 and also notes ALDH2 numbering (504 full-length; 487 mature) (register flag rv-ch73-adh1b-direction).

Ch. 73 Hit 6 says poor and ultrarapid metabolizers “need dose adjustments” for tricyclics and SSRIs. CPIC (Hicks 2017; Bousman 2023) often recommends avoiding the drug and choosing an alternative (tricyclics in CYP2D6 UM/PM; tertiary amines in CYP2C19 UM/RM; citalopram/escitalopram in CYP2C19 UM; paroxetine in CYP2D6 UM). Recommendations are guideline-specific (CPIC) (register flag rv-ch73-antidepressant-alt-drug).

Ch. 73 Hit 9 places DGKH under lithium pharmacogenomics. Baum 2008 identified DGKH in a case-control GWAS of bipolar disorder risk, not a lithium-response study; the link to lithium is through the pathway (Alda 2015: no lithium-response genetic finding replicated in two samples of 200 or more). The claim that lithium is the only mood stabilizer thoroughly examined pharmacogenomically was not verified and is not taught (register flag rv-ch73-dgkh-lithium).
